notes.meaning: Jesus answers the disciples' question about who can be saved. On our own, no human has the strength or goodness to enter God's kingdom. But God's grace can change human hearts and do what people cannot do for themselves.

Peter points out that he and the other disciples walked away from their homes and jobs to follow Jesus. He wanted to know what would become of them after giving up so much. Jesus does not scold Peter, but uses the question to encourage them all.

Jesus promises that anyone who leaves family or land for Him will be richly rewarded in this life and forever. This does not mean getting a hundred literal mothers, but gaining the love and support of God's wider spiritual family. Even so, these earthly blessings will also come with hard times and persecution.

Jesus warns that earthly rank does not match rank in the kingdom of God. Those who seem most important or honored in this world may end up last, while humble people who are overlooked will be honored. Disciples must never follow Christ just to bargain for high status.

Jesus walked boldly ahead of His disciples on the road up to Jerusalem. The disciples were amazed and frightened because they knew the leaders in the city wanted to kill Him. To prepare them, Jesus pulled the twelve apostles aside to explain what was coming.

Jesus spells out exactly how He will suffer and die. He explains that Jewish leaders will hand Him over to the Romans, who will mock, whip, and kill Him. Even with these dark details, He ends with the promise that He will rise from the dead on the third day.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars argue that Jesus could not have foretold these events in such exact detail, claiming the church added these specifics after the crucifixion took place.

notes.meaning: James and John come to Jesus with a selfish request. They ask Him to promise to give them whatever they want before they even say what it is. They were still expecting Jesus to set up an earthly royal court.

When Jesus asks what they want, the brothers ask to sit at His right and left hands in His glory. In a royal palace, those were the seats of highest honor and power. They were seeking personal greatness right after Jesus had just predicted His suffering and death.

Jesus tells James and John that they do not understand what they are asking for. He asks if they can drink His cup and share in His baptism, using these pictures to describe deep inward sorrow and outward suffering. The path to glory in God's kingdom leads through suffering, not worldly honor.

James and John quickly answer that they can, not realizing how heavy the burden will be. Jesus gently tells them that they really will share in His sufferings. James would later be killed for his faith, and John would face long years of persecution and exile.

Jesus explains that the places of highest honor are not handed out through personal favoritism. Those seats belong to the ones for whom the Father has prepared them. Followers of Christ must focus on being faithful in trials rather than grasping for special rewards.

When the other ten disciples hear about the request, they become angry with James and John. Their anger showed that they were just as concerned about position and rank as the two brothers were. None of them had yet grasped the humble nature of Jesus' kingdom.

Jesus gathers all twelve disciples together to correct their thinking about power. In the surrounding nations, rulers love to push people around and show off their authority over others. Worldly power is often used to control people rather than care for them.

Jesus tells His followers that leadership among them must be completely different from the world's ways. Anyone who wants to be truly great must choose to be a helper to everyone else. The person who desires first place must be willing to act like a humble servant of all.

Jesus points to His own mission as the ultimate example of humble service. He did not come to earth to be waited on, but to serve others and give His life as a ransom, which is a price paid to free captives from sin. His death in our place provides both our salvation and our pattern for living.

differ.view: Christ gave His life as an effective ransom specifically for the elect whom God chose to save.
Christ offered His life as a ransom sufficient for all human souls who needed redemption.

notes.meaning: As Jesus and a large crowd left Jericho, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus was sitting beside the road. Because he could not see, he had no way to earn a living except by asking travelers for help. He was in a helpless condition right along the path where Jesus was passing by.

When Bartimaeus hears that Jesus is near, he shouts out, calling Him the Son of David and begging for mercy. The crowd tells him to be quiet, but he only yells louder. He recognizes Jesus as the promised Messiah and refuses to let anyone keep him away.

Hearing the blind man's cry, Jesus stops in His tracks and tells the crowd to call him over. The people then encourage Bartimaeus to cheer up and get to his feet because the Master wants him. Jesus never treats the cry of a needy person as an unwanted interruption.

Bartimaeus immediately throws off his outer coat, leaps up, and comes to Jesus. He casts his garment aside so nothing will trip him or slow him down as he hurries forward. His quick response shows his eager faith and complete expectation of receiving help.

Jesus asks Bartimaeus what he wants Him to do, giving the beggar a chance to speak from his heart. The blind man calls Jesus his Master and asks for his eyesight to be restored. Unlike the disciples who asked for high positions, this man simply asks for mercy and light.

Jesus tells Bartimaeus that his faith has healed him, and the man receives his sight at once. Instead of simply going home, Bartimaeus follows Jesus down the road toward Jerusalem. When Christ opens our spiritual eyes, our natural response is to follow Him wherever He leads.
